title: Ignite Labs — Developer Onboard: SDK + Auth Runbook
summary: Intro + live walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, auth patterns for CI and multiple environments, demo of Console sandbox, and Optimize suggestions for latency/cost tradeoffs. Agreed to follow-up poc scoping and get a sandbox API key and sample repo.
next_steps: Priya to send sandbox API key + quickstart repo link by 2025-10-18
Ignite to confirm POC objectives and traffic profile by 2025-10-22
Schedule POC scoping call week of 2025-10-27
action_items: Priya Desai - share sandbox creds + example mono-repo (py/ts) - due 2025-10-18
Daniel Park - provide sample throughput targets and token distribution - due 2025-10-22
Alex Chen - draft pricing estimate for a 3-month Dedicated pilot - due 2025-10-21
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-16 14:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Desai, Daniel Park, Sofia Martinez, Lina Zhou

00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, Alex from Redwood — thanks for making time. Um, we'll do a quick agenda, then dive into a hands-on SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, cover auth patterns and the Console sandbox, and end with Optimize tips and next steps. Sound good?

00:14 Daniel Park: Yeah that sounds great. Quick note — Sofia's joining for the first 20 minutes and then she has another meeting.

00:21 Sofia Martinez: Hi all — jumping in. We're really keen to understand how this will fit into our CI/CD workflows and data residency stuff.

00:30 Priya Desai: Awesome — we'll call out the CI secrets patterns and the VPC/private options too. Um, for the demo I'll share my screen and run both the Python quickstart and a small TypeScript example.

00:45 Alex Chen: Quick qualification — can you remind us where you're planning to run inference today? Hosted, on-prem, or hybrid?

00:53 Daniel Park: Right now it's all in-house, we run a kube cluster and an internal model-serving layer. We're evaluating whether to keep serving models ourselves or move to managed inference. Main constraints are latency under 120ms p95 for short prompts and tight cost control.

01:10 Priya Desai: Got it. That latency target is reasonable — we'll show how batching and cache policies can be tuned so you don't lose that SLO. Also we'll discuss Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs.

01:28 Lina Zhou: Question — we have strict secrets policies, CI can't see long-lived API keys. How do you recommend rotating keys and integrating with our Vault?

01:36 Priya Desai: Good question. Typical pattern is to use short-lived tokens via our sandbox or exchange tokens from your KMS. We support KMS/HSM integration and recommend storing long-lived credentials in the Vault, then issuing ephemeral tokens in CI using the Redwood token exchange API. We'll share an example GitHub Actions step.

01:58 Alex Chen: Ok jumping into the code. I'm going to paste the Python quickstart command in chat: pip install redwood-sdk (note: the package name here might be a placeholder in transcript).

02:10 Priya Desai: I'm running a tiny script: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_KEY')); resp = client.generate('Write a one-sentence summary of product usage'); print(resp.text)

02:28 Daniel Park: Cool. Does the SDK stream events? We need streaming for our chat UI.

02:35 Priya Desai: Yes, the SDK supports streaming. In Python you can iterate over client.stream_generate(...) and in TypeScript it's event-based with async iterators. Streaming works with our Console so you can debug token timing too.

02:45 Sofia Martinez: I saw in the docs something about function calling and structured outputs — is that stable? We're going to rely on a schema to fill forms.

02:54 Priya Desai: Function/tool calling is supported — we call it tool-calls in some older places in the docs, so you might see variant names. It lets you return JSON and map to your schema. There's also a validation layer in the Console for outputs.

03:10 Alex Chen: Switching to the TypeScript example; I'll open a basic node project. npm install @redwood/sdk (again package name fuzzy in transcribe) and here's a snippet: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY }); const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'rwd-3-small', input: 'Summarize...' });

03:38 Daniel Park: That model name — rwd-3-small — is that a hosted Redwood model? We plan to bring our own model sometimes.

03:44 Priya Desai: Yes rwd-3-small is one of the verified catalog models. You can also point the SDK at a private model in your Dedicated or Private deployment. There's a model alias layer so you can switch models without changing code.

04:02 Lina Zhou: For private deployments, do you manage the control plane or is it customer-managed?

04:08 Alex Chen: For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane option. You get the Console and telemetry but you host the runtime in your VPC or on-prem; we integrate with your KMS and audit logs.

04:22 Daniel Park: Good. Walk us through the auth example for CI.

04:27 Priya Desai: Sure. Typical pattern: store long-lived credential in HashiCorp Vault; CI job requests an ephemeral token via an internal service or via Redwood's token exchange endpoint; that token is short-lived (e.g., 1 hour) and injected as REDWOOD_KEY into the job. For local dev, devs can use a local short-lived key from the Console or a developer sandbox key. We'll attach a sample GitHub Actions snippet in the follow-up.

04:55 Sofia Martinez: Any RBAC? We need to limit which services can call generation endpoints and which can only create embeddings.

05:02 Priya Desai: Yes we support token scoping and role-based policies. In the Console you can create route-level permissions, and tokens can be limited to only embeddings, or only certain models, and you can also scope to rate limits.

05:18 Alex Chen: Okay, next I'm going to bring up the Redwood Console sandbox we provisioned for Ignite. One moment — sharing screen.

05:30 [screen share noise]

05:36 Priya Desai: Here in the Console you can see the Sandbox project: Activity, API keys, Quickstart links. I'm clicking the Quickstart repo which contains a mono-repo with py and ts examples and a GitHub Actions workflow. That repo link will be in the follow-up email.

06:02 Daniel Park: Nice — I see usage limits and a token breakdown. Does the Console show per-route latency percentiles?

06:09 Priya Desai: Yes, per-route dashboards with p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and you can correlate with request tracing IDs. We also surface KV cache hit rates when enabled.

06:22 Lina Zhou: About caching — can prefix caching be used without violating user privacy with PII? We need to ensure we don't cache any user-identifying strings across tenants.

06:33 Priya Desai: Absolutely — caching policies are configurable by route and you can redact sensitive fields before caching. For multi-tenant setups we'd recommend tenant-scoped caches or disabling prefix caching for PII routes.

06:48 Sofia Martinez: We have a questions about model rollouts. If a new quantized model is cheaper but lower quality, can Redwood do canary rollouts?

06:57 Alex Chen: Yes, rollouts are built-in: you can do traffic splits per model version or fallbacks to a higher-quality variant if quality degrades. The Console will alert regressions tied to a prompt set.

07:10 Daniel Park: Great. Let's talk about Optimize — you're recommending batching/caching — any heuristics for our chat-like workload?

07:20 Priya Desai: For chat where latency is important, use small micro-batches (e.g., 8-16) and aggressive KV caching for repeated context. For embedding-heavy pipelines, batch larger with async pools. We'll give a recommended profile based on the sample traffic you provide.

07:38 Alex Chen: Quick demo of a small benchmark script I run in the repo: it uses the SDK and hits the sandbox with a tokenized payload distribution that matches a 3-turn chat. Results show 95ms median, 140ms p95 with default settings — we can tune batching to hit your 120ms p95.

07:58 Lina Zhou: You've mentioned quantization — do you handle quantized models in Hosted? Any lock-in?

08:06 Priya Desai: We support quantized variants in both Hosted and Dedicated; quantized models are model variants so it's easy to switch. There's no lock-in — you can export model configs and run them in your private infra if you choose.

08:22 Daniel Park: Ok, stopping screen share. For the code samples, what about telemetry and logging? We need request IDs to tie back to our logs.

08:30 Priya Desai: The SDK automatically returns a request_id header and you can attach custom metadata. The Console ingest shows traces and lets you search by request_id and user token. We'll show an example log snippet: RequestID: rwd-abc123, model: rwd-3-small, latency_ms: 118

08:50 Sofia Martinez: (overlap) also audit logs for admin actions — we need them to go into our SIEM.

08:55 Alex Chen: Audit logs can be exported via syslog or S3 and you can plug them into your SIEM. For Private deployments you have full control.

09:05 Daniel Park: Let's talk about limits — sandbox vs prod. If we start with sandbox and then move to Dedicated, what is the onboarding time?

09:12 Priya Desai: Sandbox is immediate. Dedicated provisioning is typically 2-4 weeks depending on region and GPU availability; Dedicated also includes reserved capacity and SLA. We'll put a timeline in the follow-up.

09:25 Lina Zhou: Are there any compliance certs we should be aware of? SOC2? ISO?

09:30 Alex Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II and are working on ISO 27001 for certain regions; we'll share our security package.

09:36 Daniel Park: (note of transition) okay Sofia needs to drop now — thanks for joining.

09:40 Sofia Martinez: Thanks everyone — follow-up with the security packet would be great. Bye.

09:45 [Sofia leaves]

09:50 Alex Chen: Back to the demo — Priya, can you run the TypeScript streaming example to show how message-by-message comes through?

09:58 Priya Desai: Sure — running node stream-demo.js. This will stream tokens for a 50-token response. (background typing) You'll see in the console it prints partial chunks, then final event. There's also a callback hook so you can send partial render events to your UI.

10:25 Daniel Park: Looks good. One more question — do you have limits on max context length and how to handle long documents?

10:32 Priya Desai: Max context varies by model family. For long documents we recommend chunking + retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Redwood has built-in embeddings endpoints and you can use our reranker to filter candidate passages. For very long context we also support model-specific streaming of KV cache to disk in Dedicated environments.

10:55 Daniel Park: Let's cover billing. How granular is usage reporting? We need per-team cost chargeback.

11:03 Alex Chen: The Console has token-level billing and you can tag routes and API keys to map usage to teams. We also expose an API for exports so you can run chargeback scripts nightly.

11:18 Lina Zhou: Quick follow — are there example policies for redaction we can apply?

11:24 Priya Desai: Yes, the repo includes a small redaction middleware for Node + Python that strips PII patterns before sending. We'll attach it.

11:35 Daniel Park: Ok, I think that's a solid demo. For the follow-up POC scoping, we'll share expected qps, typical prompt lengths, and required compliance items.

11:45 Alex Chen: Great. Recap of next steps: Priya will send sandbox key and repo; Alex will draft a pilot price; Ignite will provide traffic profile; we'll schedule POC scoping the week of 10/27. Any final questions?

11:58 Lina Zhou: No, thanks — this was helpful.

12:05 Priya Desai: I'll also include the GitHub Actions snippet and the token exchange example.

12:12 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in the email.

12:18 [meeting ends]
